$comment: The engine-neutrality ratchet. One entry per directory under src/, recording how much of it
still names a JavaScript engine directly. scripts/check-engine-neutrality.sh measures the tree
and compares it against these numbers.
THESE NUMBERS MAY FALL AND MAY NEVER RISE. A count above its budget fails the build, and the
fix is to port the file rather than to raise the number. A migration that moves a file onto
Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal lowers a count, and must lower the budget in the SAME COMMIT -- the
check reports every count that came in under budget for exactly that reason, because a ratchet
nobody tightens is a ratchet that stops at whatever the worst day was.
THE ONE RISE THAT IS NOT A REGRESSION IS A CHANGE TO THE METRIC, AND THERE HAS BEEN ONE.
engineReferences used to count only the string 'Broiler.JavaScript'. Every project under src/
has a RootNamespace beginning 'Broiler.', so 'JavaScript.Runtime.JSObject' compiles and means
the same thing -- and 23 real references in Broiler.HtmlBridge.Dom were spelled that way,
invisible to the check, concentrated in exactly the files mid-migration where somebody had
dropped a using and qualified what was left. The count now sees both spellings. Dom's recorded
number therefore went 108 -> 111 in the commit that widened it while its actual coupling FELL by
18 in the same commit, and both halves of that sentence are the point: a number may rise when
the instrument improves, and it may never rise because the tree got worse. A commit doing the
first says so here.
The consequence worth stating plainly: a project whose budget is already 0 cannot gain an
engine-coupled file at all. That is the state every entry here is travelling towards, and it
is what lets the remaining migration land as a hundred small changes instead of one merge that
moves 250 files and can only be reviewed by trusting it.
Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal is 0/0/0 and is the one entry these numbers do not actually protect.
Its project file has no ProjectReference and no PackageReference, so an assembly that cannot
see a Broiler.JavaScript type cannot name one: its neutrality is a compiler outcome, not a grep
result. What the check guards there is the CLAIM -- it fails if that project file ever gains a
reference of either kind, because the moment it does, every 0 below stops meaning anything.
WHAT EACH METRIC COUNTS, LITERALLY.
engineReferences   Occurrences of the text 'Broiler.JavaScript' in .cs files beneath the
directory, bin/ and obj/ excluded. Text, not semantics: a using directive,
a fully-qualified type name and a mention inside a doc comment each count
one. Counting occurrences rather than files is deliberate -- a file being
half-ported is progress, and a metric that only moved when a whole file
landed would hide it.
engineProjectRefs  Direct engine dependencies declared in .csproj files, regardless of
Condition: ProjectReference paths into Broiler.JS/ or Broiler.VM/
(including root-property paths), plus Broiler.JavaScript.* and
Broiler.VM.* PackageReferences. The historical name is retained.
A zero does not rule out engine dependencies arriving transitively.
guestEvalSites     Occurrences of '.Eval(' in .cs files. The name records where these are
going, not what they are: today's sites are undifferentiated, and splitting
them into IJsSource.EvaluateHostScript (source this repository authored,
exempt from the page's content policy) and EvaluateClassicScript (a script
the page carries, which script-src governs) is the porting work this number
measures for a binding's sites; a provider's own evaluation and Dom's module
probe are counted as well and are not that work (see their notes). None goes to
EvaluateDynamicSource (what the page asks to evaluate at run time, which
'unsafe-eval' governs): no counted site evaluates text the page asks for at run
time, and the page's own eval and Function are refused inside the realm rather
than through that member. A ported site no longer names .Eval(, so it leaves
this count; engineReferences counts namespace text, so it falls only when a
port also deletes a using or qualified name the file no longer needs.
WHY THE UNIT IS A DIRECTORY AND NOT A PROJECT FILE. src/Broiler.App has no .csproj: its eight
files are pulled in by <Compile Include="..\Broiler.App\..."> from three heads. Keying this
on project files would leave those files counted nowhere, which is the one place an engine
reference could be parked without any budget noticing. Keying on the directory covers them, and
makes the entry name the same string the check prints.
This is an object rather than the array eng/solutions.json uses, so that a directory cannot be
budgeted twice -- two entries for one project would let the check read whichever came first.

A project marked "role": "provider" is the one kind whose engine references are SUPPOSED to grow -- naming the engine is what a provider assembly is for. For those, engineReferences and guestEvalSites are recorded and reported when they drift, but not enforced; engineProjectRefs stays enforced, because which engine assemblies a provider links is a real boundary and a Broiler.JS provider quietly acquiring a Broiler.VM reference should have to argue for it in a diff.

MOVED OUT OF Broiler.Browser ON 2026-09-16, WITH THE CODE IT BUDGETS. Seven entries went away in that move and none of them was a project this ratchet was ever about: Broiler.App, Broiler.App.Android, Broiler.Browser.Android, Broiler.Browser.Core, Broiler.Browser.Core.Tests, Broiler.Browser.Linux and Broiler.Browser.Windows. Six of the seven were at 0/0/0 and stayed in the browser; the seventh, Broiler.Browser.Core, carries one unconditional Broiler.JavaScript.All reference because BrowserApp.NewScriptEngine() still picks an engine with an #if rather than through JsEngineRegistry. That is now a fact about an EMBEDDER rather than about the bridge, which is the right place for it to be argued, and it is no longer measured here because this check deliberately does not look outside its own src/.
After the NuGet migration, the guard counts engine packages as well as legacy project paths. Switching dependency delivery mechanisms must not appear to remove engine coupling.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Core.note: ONE FILE, ONE LINE, AND IT IS THE SEAM. The single reference is `using Broiler.JavaScript.Engine;` in Dom/IDomBridgeRuntime.cs, and the only thing it serves is the pair of Attach overloads that take a JSContext. This was 3 across two files until ScriptCompileAhead.cs was deleted -- 327 lines with no caller anywhere in the tree, whose two usings were the other 2. What that removal buys is not the count: it means engineProjectRefs 1, the ProjectReference to Broiler.JavaScript.Engine, is now held by exactly one API in one file, so an Attach that takes an IJsRealm drops the reference in the same commit rather than turning up a second dependency behind it. This is the highest-value entry in the file despite being the smallest -- an Attach a second engine can call is what makes a second engine able to serve a page at all. Note for whoever ports it: Broiler.JS's own docs/roadmap/Modernization.md MOD-M5 names the deleted file as an import source, so it is taken from this repository's history rather than from the tree.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Dom.note: The remaining direct engine dependency is the Broiler.JavaScript.Modules package. Core brings the engine transitively.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.DomBridgeUtils.note: The bridge's static helpers that need no bridge instance, moved out of Broiler.HtmlBridge.Dom. It references Core and Jseal and no engine project, and it arrived at zero because the one helper that names the engine, AdoptRealm (JSContext), stayed in Dom as DomBridgeHostUtils together with its using line -- so Dom's 12 did not move either. A helper that needs the engine belongs in DomBridgeHostUtils, not here.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal.note: Proved by the compiler, not by this file. The project has no ProjectReference and no PackageReference, so it cannot name an engine type whatever a grep says; the check fails if that project file ever gains one. See the comment in Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal.csproj.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal.BroilerJs.note: The Broiler.JS provider, and the one project under src/ whose budget is not expected to reach zero. Naming Broiler.JavaScript is what this assembly is for: every reference here is a reference the bridge no longer has to make. The single eval site is JSContext.Eval inside the realm's own IJsSource implementation -- the provider being asked to evaluate, not a binding evaluating. Its engine project references were Broiler.JavaScript.Engine and .BuiltIns until IJsClone landed and took engineProjectRefs from 2 to 3: JSGlobalStatic.StructuredClone lives in Broiler.JavaScript.Globals, so the provider that implements structured clone needs it. That is the gate doing its job rather than a regression -- the same reference LEFT Broiler.HtmlBridge.Dom in the same commit, because the bridge's only use of it was the call that is now behind the contract. An engine assembly reached by the provider and not by the bridge is the shape all of these should end in.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal.Vm.note: VM provider: three direct packages (Profile.JavaScript, Profile.JavaScript.Compiler and Runtime). Abstractions and Binary arrive transitively. The source-reference metric counts Broiler.JS namespaces, not Broiler.VM.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Scripting.note: No direct engine package or project references; engine types still arrive through Core and Jseal.BroilerJs. Source references and evaluation sites remain budgeted.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Scripting.Vm.note: No direct engine package or project references; VM types arrive through Jseal.Vm. This does not mean its transitive closure is engine-neutral.
